text:
A starter that goes flat and sluggish has usually run out of food. Say the colony of wild yeast and lactobacilli is fed once, then left for days on a warm 26°C counter. It uses up the sugars in the flour within roughly 8-12 hours. After that, acid builds up faster than gas. Lactic and acetic acids pull the pH below about 3.8. Yeast tolerates acid far less than the bacteria do, so it stalls, while the bacteria keep souring the starter and the bubbles stop.

Hooch, the grey layer of alcohol that pools on top, shows that the culture has used up its food. Two other causes are chlorinated tap water, which can bleach a young colony, and cold storage near 4°C, which slows fermentation to a crawl.

The fix is to keep the feeding ratios strict. Discard most of the starter, then feed it starter, flour and water at 1:2:2 every twelve hours. With fresh starch and less acid, the starter typically recovers and doubles again within two or three feedings.
